title_en: Xu Wenqing v. Patent Reexamination Board of the National Intellectual Property Administration and Third Party Xing Pengwan — dispute over a decision declaring an invention patent invalid
ruling_gist_en: (1) When examining a request for a declaration of invalidity of a patent, the Patent Reexamination Board shall provide the parties in the proceeding with an appropriate opportunity to explain and present their arguments on the relevant specific facts, reasons, and evidence, especially before making a decision adverse to the parties. Failure to do so constitutes a violation of the hearing principle in patent reexamination proceedings, which falls under the circumstance of "violation of statutory procedures" as provided in Article 54, paragraph (2), item 3 of the Administrative Procedure Law.

full_text_en:
Xu Wenqing v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office and Third Party Xing Pengwan — Dispute over Decision Declaring Invention Patent Invalid

Ruling Summary

(I) When examining a request for declaring a patent right invalid, the Patent Reexamination Board shall afford the parties in the proceedings an appropriate opportunity to explain and state reasons regarding the specific facts, reasons, and evidence involved, especially before making a decision adverse to a party. Otherwise, it violates the principle of hearing in patent reexamination and constitutes a circumstance of "violating statutory procedures" as specified in Article 54(2)(3) of the Administrative Procedure Law.

(II) In determining whether a patent claim is supported by the description, the main consideration shall be whether each technical solution claimed for protection in the claims can be directly obtained or derived by a person of ordinary skill in the art from the content disclosed in the description, and whether the scope of the claims exceeds the content recorded in the description.

Administrative Judgment of the Supreme People's Court (Summary)

(2005) Min San Ti Zi No. 2

Applicant for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Xu Wenqing, male, Han ethnicity, born June 4, 1938, factory director and senior engineer of Mudanjiang Petrochemical Container Equipment Anticorrosion Factory, Heilongjiang Province, domiciled at No. 31 Fu Group, 1 Wei, Daqing Office, Yangming District, Mudanjiang City, Heilongjiang Province.

Agent ad litem: Liu Ying, lawyer of Mudanjiang Tianyuan Law Firm, Heilongjiang Province.

Agent ad litem: Wu Zhongren, male, Han ethnicity, born November 14, 1937, patent agent of Beijing Shuangshou Intellectual Property Agency Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 102, Door 1, Building 28, Anxiangli, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Respondent to the Application for Retrial (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office, domiciled at No. 6 Xitucheng Road, Jimenqiao West, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Liao Tao, Deputy Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Chai Aijun, examiner of the Administrative Litigation Review Division of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Cui Guozhen, examiner of the Administrative Litigation Review Division of the Board.

Third Party at First Instance: Xing Pengwan, male, Han ethnicity, born June 2, 1959, general manager of Hailin Anticorrosion Company, Heilongjiang Province, domiciled at 32nd Wei, Hailin Town, Hailin City, Heilongjiang Province.

Agent ad litem: Li Qingsong, lawyer of Beijing Shengzhi Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Liu Hong, female, Han ethnicity, born April 16, 1979, legal counsel of Hailin Anticorrosion Company, Heilongjiang Province, domiciled at No. 161-4, Xiqing Road, Hongqiao District, Tianjin.

In the dispute between the applicant for retrial Xu Wenqing and the respondent to the application for retrial, the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board), and the third party at first instance Xing Pengwan, concerning the decision declaring the invention patent invalid, the Beijing High People's Court rendered the second-instance administrative judgment (2000) Gao Zhi Zhong Zi No. 72 on April 9, 2001, which became legally effective. Xu Wenqing, dissatisfied with that judgment, applied to this Court for retrial. On March 28, 2005, this Court decided to conduct a retrial of this case by administrative ruling (2001) Min San Jian Zi No. 20-1. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, with trial judge Wang Yongchang serving as the presiding judge, acting trial judges He Zhonglin and Li Jian participating in the deliberation, and Cui Lina serving as the clerk of this case. On April 15, 2005, the parties exchanged evidence and clarified the main issues in dispute in this case. On April 21 and August 5, 2005, the collegial panel held a public hearing of this case. Xu Wenqing and his agents ad litem Liu Ying and Wu Zhongren, the agents ad litem of the Patent Reexamination Board Chai Aijun and Cui Guozhen, and Xing Pengwan and his agents ad litem Li Qingsong and Liu Hong appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

The Beijing High People's Court found: On June 8, 1988, Xu Wenqing filed with the Chinese Patent Office an invention patent application entitled "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles," which was granted the patent right on March 6, 1991, with patent number 88103519X. The claims of the invention patent were:

1. A method for anticorrosion of the inner and outer walls of steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers, that is, to first form a phosphating layer on the inner and outer wall surfaces of the steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers, and then perform coating; characterized in that this process is accomplished by adopting (a) connecting the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger, pump, valve group, and solution tank through rubber tubes and iron tubes according to the process flow to form a closed-circuit circulation system; (b) various treatment liquids (alkali liquid, acid liquid, phosphating liquid) used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger throughout the entire process flow being in a state of continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow.

2. The process flow steps of claim 1 for first forming a phosphating layer on the inner wall surface of the steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger and then performing coating include: (1) sandblasting; (2) acid pickling; (3) neutralization; (4) phosphating; (5) drying; (6) coating.

3. The process flow steps of claim 1 for first forming a phosphating layer on the outer wall surface of the steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger and then performing coating adopt chemical degreasing to replace the step of sandblasting, with the remaining steps being identical to those described in claim 2.

4. In the coating step of claim 2 or 3, the amount of coating material used is two-thirds of the volume of the tube side or the shell side.

The specification of the invention patent stated that this method for anticorrosion of inner and outer walls of metal steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers in industries such as petroleum and chemicals belongs to a new process for metal anticorrosion. It also stated that currently, tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers in the petroleum and chemical industries can only have their inner walls sandblasted (or chemically treated), and then be coated with organic coatings (epoxy phenolic, 7910, CH784, etc.). The coating adheres to the metal tube based on adhesive force, forming a passivation film on the metal surface. This anticorrosion treatment method results in poor bonding between the coating and the metal steel substrate; after coating, a trace amount of moisture can permeate, generating oxides on the metal surface, causing the coating film to blister, crack, and peel off, and the substrate to corrode; it is resistant to high-temperature media below 150°C, and the anticorrosion treatment period is long. The concept of the present invention is: after sandblasting the inner and outer walls of tube bundles of large-scale complex structural equipment in the petroleum and chemical industries to remove the oxide scale, and with the aid of pumps, valves, pipelines, and solution tanks connected and operated according to the process flow, first form a phosphating layer on the inner and outer walls of the tube bundle, and then select coatings with different physical and chemical properties according to different medium requirements and different temperature requirements.

The specification disclosed an embodiment, recording the following technical solution: after rust removal and sandblasting of the inner wall of the cooler tube according to conventional techniques, connect auxiliary equipment such as pumps, valves, pipelines, and solution tanks according to the process flow diagram. The anticorrosion process steps for the inner wall of the cooler tube disclosed in this embodiment include: (1) acid pickling; (2) neutralization; (3) phosphating; (4) rinsing the inner wall with clean water, then blowing with compressed air; (5) drying; (6) coating. The embodiment also disclosed that the anticorrosion treatment of the outer wall of the tube differs from the inner wall treatment in four aspects: (1) connecting the pump outlet to the shell-side inlet, and the shell-side outlet to the respective solution tanks; (2) alkaline washing for chemical degreasing, with alkaline washing for 45 minutes at a temperature of 70–90°C; (3) after alkaline washing, washing with hot water, then washing with cold water; (4) drying, by introducing steam from the tube-side outlet of the cooler.

On March 28, 1997, Xing Pengwan filed a request with the Patent Reexamination Board for declaring the invention patent "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" invalid, on the ground that the invention patent did not comply with the provisions of Article 22(2) and (3) of the Patent Law. On April 13, 1998, in a written opinion statement, Xing Pengwan further stated that the invention patent did not comply with the provisions of Article 26(4) of the Patent Law.

On June 17, 1998, the Patent Reexamination Board received a request for declaring the invention patent "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" invalid submitted by Daqing Honggang District Jinxing Anticorrosion Company (hereinafter referred to as Jinxing Company). Jinxing Company believed that the invention patent did not comply with the provisions of Article 26(4), Article 22(3), Article 22(4), and Article 26(3) of the Patent Law.

The Patent Reexamination Board consolidated these two invalidation request cases for trial, and on December 22, 1998, issued a notice of oral hearing to be held on March 10, 1999. The main issues involved in the oral hearing were whether the patent complied with Article 26(4) and Article 22(2) and (3) of the Patent Law.

During the oral hearing on March 10, 1999, the parties presented their opinions on whether the invention patent "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" complied with the provisions of the Patent Law.

On June 4, 1999, the Patent Reexamination Board made Decision No. 1372 on the Request for Declaration of Invalidity, declaring Xu Wenqing's invention patent No. 88103519X "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" invalid on the ground that the claims were not supported by the description.

Xu Wenqing, dissatisfied with Decision No. 1372 of the Patent Reexamination Board, filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Xu Wenqing's assertions that the Patent Reexamination Board violated the principle of hearing and the principle of party disposition and request were inconsistent with the facts and were not adopted. The claims of the invention patent "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" were not based on the description and did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. Xu Wenqing's reasons for the lawsuit could not stand, and his claims for the lawsuit were not supported. The court rendered a judgment: rejecting Xu Wenqing's claims and maintaining Decision No. 1372 on the Request for Declaration of Invalidity. The case acceptance fee of 800 yuan was borne by Xu Wenqing.

Xu Wenqing, dissatisfied with the judgment of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. The Beijing High People's Court found after trial that during the trial process, the Patent Reexamination Board transferred evidentiary materials and opinion statements to the invalidation requester and the patentee in accordance with the regulations, and stated in the oral hearing notice that the scope of the oral hearing included whether the invention patent "A Method for Anticorrosion of Inner and Outer Walls of Steel Tube Bundles" complied with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. Xu Wenqing also made statements on this issue in his written defense opinion to the Patent Reexamination Board's oral hearing. Xu Wenqing's grounds of appeal could not stand. The court, in accordance with Article 54(1)(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered a judgment: dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. The court costs for the first and second instances were borne by Xu Wenqing.

Xu Wenqing, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to this Court for retrial, requesting this Court to revoke Decision No. 1372 of the Patent Reexamination Board and the judgments of the first- and second-instance courts, maintain the validity of the patent, and order the Patent Reexamination Board to bear all litigation costs of this case. The main reasons for his application for retrial were:

(I) Decision No. 1372 of the Patent Reexamination Board violated the principle of hearing and the principle of party request as stipulated in the Guidelines for Examination. (II) The determination in Decision No. 1372 that the claims of the patent in question were not supported by the description lacked sufficient evidence and involved erroneous application of laws and regulations.

The Patent Reexamination Board responded with the following reasons:

(I) In the invalidation review procedure for the patent in question, the Respondent fully complied with the principle of request and the principle of hearing.

(II) Claim 1 requests protection of a method for anticorrosion of the inner and outer walls of steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers, the content of which is not recorded in text in the description. According to the clearly recorded content in the description that the anticorrosion treatment for the inner wall of the tube bundle and the anticorrosion treatment for the outer wall of the tube bundle are two different technical solutions, it is difficult for a person of ordinary skill in the art to obtain the technical solution as described in Claim 1 after reading the description. Based on the same reasoning, dependent Claims 2 and 3, and dependent Claim 4, are also naturally not supported by the description, and do not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. Therefore, the determination in Decision No. 1372 that Claims 1 to 4 of the patent in question are not supported by the description is correct.

Upon trial, this Court finds that the facts found by the original trial court are basically true, but other parts of the facts of this case were omitted. This Court further finds:

(I) Facts regarding whether Decision No. 1372 violated the principle of hearing and the principle of party request.

1. On March 28, 1997, Xing Pengwan filed a request with the Patent Reexamination Board for declaring the patent right in this case invalid, on the grounds that the patent did not comply with Article 22(2) and (4) of the Patent Law, i.e., lack of novelty and inventiveness, without involving the issue of whether the claims were supported by the description under Article 26(4) of the Patent Law.

2. On April 13, 1998, the Patent Reexamination Board received a written opinion statement from Xing Pengwan. In that written opinion statement, Xing Pengwan raised the reason that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. Specifically: the distinguishing feature (b) of Claim 1 could not find an identical description in the specification, nor could it clearly and accurately support this distinguishing technical feature; therefore, Claim 1 was not supported by the description, and the remaining dependent Claims 2 to 4 were all dependent on Claim 1 and naturally were also not supported by the description.

On October 30 of the same year, the Patent Reexamination Board received a written opinion statement submitted by Xu Wenqing. In that written opinion statement, Xu Wenqing responded to Xing Pengwan's reason that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, stating: the distinguishing feature (b) part of Claim 1 of the present invention was supported by the description.

3. On November 23, 1998, Xing Pengwan again submitted to the Patent Reexamination Board "Facts and Reasons for Declaring the Patent Right Invalid," in which, in the part concerning the reason that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, it was recorded: "Completing this process is accomplished by adopting connecting the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger, pump, valve, solution tank through rubber tubes and iron tubes according to the process flow to form a closed-circuit circulation system" was not supported by the description; "Completing this process is accomplished by adopting that various treatment liquids (alkali liquid, acid liquid, phosphating liquid) used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger throughout the entire process flow are in a state of continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow" was not sufficiently disclosed in the description.

4. On June 17, 1998, the Patent Reexamination Board received a "Request for Declaration of Patent Right Invalidity" submitted by third-party Jinxing Company. Among the specific reasons concerning non-compliance with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law were: the feature "closed circuit" in feature (a) was not described in the description, and a person of ordinary skill in the art, after reading the description, could not infer that it was a closed-circuit circulation system; feature (b) required that various treatment liquids be in a state of continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow, but there was no description of such a technical feature in the description, and a person of ordinary skill in the art, after reading the description, might not necessarily think of making various treatment liquids in a state of continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow.

5. On December 22, 1998, the Patent Reexamination Board issued a "Notice of Oral Hearing" to Xu Wenqing, in which, under the heading "Main Issues to be Addressed in the Oral Hearing," it stated: "Whether the patent complies with Article 26(4) and Article 22(2) and (3) of the Patent Law."

6. On March 8, 1999, in the "Outline for Requester's Oral Hearing Remarks," Xing Pengwan stated regarding the issue that the claims of the patent in question were not supported by the description: the distinguishing feature (b) of Claim 1 was "throughout the entire process flow, various treatment liquids (alkali liquid, acid liquid, phosphating liquid) used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger are in a state of continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow." However, no content clearly and accurately supporting this technical feature could be found in the description.

7. On March 10, 1999, the Patent Reexamination Board conducted an oral hearing regarding the patent in question. The Patent Reexamination Board did not provide corresponding minutes of the main process and content of the oral hearing.

8. On March 10, 1999, Xu Wenqing submitted a "Supplementary Agent's Statement (Ad litem)" to the Patent Reexamination Board. It stated: the "various treatment liquids (alkali liquid, acid liquid, phosphating liquid) used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger throughout the entire process flow" in feature (b) of Claim 1 of the patent naturally refer to the liquids used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the metal steel tube bundles of the cooler/heat exchanger. Although alkali was also used during neutralization in the patented method, the amount was small, and because its concentration was very low and contained acid radicals, there was no need for circulation. The requester's claim that the treatment liquids recorded in the claim also did not have closed-circuit circulation based on the fact that the alkali used for neutralization did not circulate was incorrect.

9. On March 15, 1999, third-party Wang Yueming filed a request with the Patent Reexamination Board for declaring the patent right in question invalid on the ground that the patent in question was not supported by the description, and submitted a "Request for Declaration of Patent Right Invalidity." The third ground for invalidity in that request was: the acid pickling (acid liquid), neutralization (alkali liquid), and phosphating (phosphating liquid) recorded in the description did not support the various treatment liquids (alkali liquid, acid liquid, phosphating liquid) in Claim 1(b).

10. On March 19, 1999, the Patent Reexamination Board received a written "Agent's Statement (Post-Oral Hearing Statement)" submitted by Xing Pengwan. It asserted that the method for anticorrosion treatment of the inner wall of the tube bundle recorded in the description was not identical to the anticorrosion method described in Claim 1, and therefore Claim 1 was not supported by the description.

The Patent Reexamination Board did not transfer this agent's statement to Xu Wenqing.

(II) Facts regarding whether the claims were based on the description

1. Facts concerning whether the technical solutions claimed for protection in Claims 1, 2, 3, and 4 could be derived from the description.

(1) Paragraph 6 of the description contains a description of the drawings.

(2) Paragraph 7 of the description contains examples of the anticorrosion treatment methods for inner and outer walls of the tube.

(3) The description includes a process flow diagram for the anticorrosion treatment of inner and outer walls of the cooler tube, illustrating the connection of steel tube bundles, pump, valve group, and solution tank through rubber tubes and iron tubes according to the process flow.

2. Facts concerning whether the process steps for forming a phosphating layer, i.e., the pre-painting surface treatment technology, were prior art.

(1) In the first volume of "Coating Technology" (edited by Wang Xichun and Jiang Yingtao, published by Chemical Industry Press in June 1986), Chapter 3 "Pre-Painting Surface Treatment" states: All preparatory work carried out on the surface of the object to be coated before painting is called pre-painting surface treatment. Pre-painting surface treatment, coating, and drying are the three main processes of the painting process.

In the section "Degreasing of Metals," it is stated: "The most commonly used pre-paint degreasing methods include alkali cleaning, organic solvent cleaning, surfactant cleaning, emulsion cleaning, etc. The selection of degreasing method depends on the nature of the oil contamination, the degree of contamination, the material of the object to be cleaned, and the method of production."

In the section "Chemical Rust Removal," the inorganic acid pickling process is introduced, with the process steps as follows: degreasing alkali tank - hot water tank - acid pickling tank - cold water tank - neutralization tank - cold water tank - phosphating tank - hot water tank - paint coating maintenance.

(2) *Electroplating Handbook* (Volume One) (compiled by the *Electroplating Handbook* Editorial Group, published by National Defense Industry Press in October 1977), in the chapter "Surface Preparation of Parts," regarding "Sandblasting Treatment," states: "Sandblasting is used to remove burrs, scale, and slag impurities from the surface of metal products. ... Sandblasting uses purified compressed air to forcefully spray a stream of dry sand onto the surface of metal products, thereby knocking off dirt on the surface. The sand used for sandblasting should be dry, and the surface of the metal product should also be dry and free of oil; otherwise, the sandblasting effect will be poor."

(3) *Electroplating Technology* (edited by the Electroplating Technology Editorial Committee of the Electroplating Workshop of State-Owned Huifeng Machinery Factory, published by Machinery Industry Press in 1959), on page 114, further provides a table introducing the process specifications for phosphating, namely: chemical degreasing - hot water washing - cold water washing - acid pickling - cold water washing - soda soap treatment - hot water washing - phosphating - hot water washing - passivation treatment - hot water washing - distilled water washing - compressed air drying - oven drying - appearance inspection - paint coating.

(4) *Modern Science and Technology Dictionary* (Volume Two) (published by Shanghai Science and Technology Press in December 1980), on page 22, explains the term "sandblasting cleaning" as follows: "A surface treatment method that involves blasting steel grit, sand, or other abrasives onto an object to create a rough surface or to remove dirt, rust, scale, etc. Uses a gas jet or liquid jet containing abrasives to remove contaminants from a solid surface."

On page 195, it explains the term "neutralization" as follows: "Adding an alkali to an acidic solution, or adding an acid to an alkaline solution, to make the solution neutral (neither acidic nor alkaline, pH 7)."

(5) In the *Main Text of Statement of Opinions* submitted by Xing Pengwan to the Patent Reexamination Board, he stated: "Common knowledge in coating technology tells us that, for corrosion protection, metal surfaces can be coated with paint. Before applying paint, the metal surface should undergo pre-paint surface treatment to remove contaminants (including oil, rust, scale, old paint, etc.), followed by phosphating treatment to form a phosphating layer on the metal surface, so that the coating bonds firmly to the metal surface. Methods for removing contaminants from metal surfaces include mechanical removal methods (e.g., sandblasting, etc.) and chemical cleaning methods, which include alkali washing and acid washing, among others. This common knowledge is found in any book on coating technology, for example, in Comparison Document 2 (i.e., the aforementioned *Coating Technology* Volume 1), especially Chapter 3 'Pre-Paint Surface Treatment,' which details the above common knowledge."

The parties have no objection to the above facts.

The Court holds that the main issues in dispute in this case are: whether Decision No. 1372 violated the principles of hearing and the parties' request as stipulated in the *Guidelines for Patent Examination*, and whether the claims of the patent in question are supported by the description.

(I) Regarding whether Decision No. 1372 violated the principles of hearing and the parties' request.

1. Regarding the violation of the principle of hearing.

The requirement under Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law that "the claims shall be based on the description" is one of the statutory conditions for the grant of a patent right. If the granted patent right does not meet the conditions set forth in that paragraph, i.e., the claims are not supported by the description, any person may request the Patent Reexamination Board to declare the patent right invalid. However, a requester seeking invalidation based on that paragraph must provide specific facts and reasons. The so-called "giving the parties in the proceedings appropriate opportunities to explain and present reasons," i.e., the principle of hearing, as stipulated in Section 8.4 of Chapter 1, Part IV of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* (1993 version), means that the parties must be given appropriate opportunities to explain and present reasons regarding these specific facts and reasons. In particular, the facts and reasons on which the examination decision is based must be given to the parties for explanation and reasoning.

From the facts ascertained by the court of first instance and the additional facts ascertained by this Court, from the time the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, and the outsider, Jinsing Company, filed the request to declare the patent in question invalid with the Patent Reexamination Board, until the conclusion of the oral hearing by the Patent Reexamination Board on March 10, 1999 regarding the declaration of invalidity of the patent in question, the main reasons asserted by the two requestors that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law can be summarized as: the "closed-loop circulation system" described in the distinguishing feature (a) of claim 1 is not described in the specification; it can be closed or not closed; the various treatment liquids described in distinguishing feature (b) are in a state of "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow," which is not described in the specification; the flow of treatment liquids is not continuous and uninterrupted. The opinions stated by the retrial applicant, Xu Wenqing, in the administrative procedure for declaring invalidity were also directed to the above grounds for invalidation. The third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, and the outsider, Jinsing Company, did not raise the invalidation grounds as set forth in the "Requestor's Contentions" section on page 4, lines 21-26 of Decision No. 1372.

From the 10th fact regarding procedural aspects ascertained by this Court as supplementary, it can be seen that the part of the invalidation grounds in Decision No. 1372 was actually summarized based on the *Agent's Arguments (Post-Oral Hearing Statement of Opinions)* submitted by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, to the Patent Reexamination Board on March 19, 1999. The substantive meaning of these contents is that claim 1 of the patent in question generalizes the anti-corrosion treatment methods for the inner and outer walls of the tube bundle into one technical solution, whereas, according to the description, the anti-corrosion treatment method for the inner wall of the tube bundle and the method for the outer wall of the tube bundle are two different technical solutions. Therefore, claim 1 is not supported by the description. Comparing the invalidation grounds raised by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, in his post-oral hearing agent's arguments—that the claims of the patent in question are not supported by the description—with the invalidation grounds previously raised by the outsider, Jinsing Company, that the claims of the patent in question are not supported by the description, the two are clearly different.

However, because this part of the invalidation grounds was raised by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, after the oral hearing, and the Patent Reexamination Board did not forward a copy of that agent's arguments to the retrial applicant, Xu Wenqing, Xu Wenqing's assertion that he did not know or was not aware of the invalidation grounds in the "Requestor's Contentions" section on page 4, lines 21-26 of Decision No. 1372 during the invalidation procedure is factually based. The Patent Reexamination Board made the decision to declare the patent in question invalid precisely based on the new invalidation grounds raised in the agent's arguments submitted by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, after the oral hearing. This is clearly stated in the fourth ground of Decision No. 1372. In contrast, the invalidation grounds raised by the requestor and for which the respondent presented opinions—i.e., that the "closed-loop circulation system" described in distinguishing feature (a) of claim 1 is not closed, and that the various treatment liquids in feature (b) are not in a "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow" state—were not addressed in Decision No. 1372. The *Guidelines for Patent Examination* is an administrative regulation formulated by the State Intellectual Property Office in accordance with the Patent Law and its Implementing Rules, which sets forth operational standards for patent grant and patent invalidation reexamination, and is binding on the Patent Reexamination Board and must be strictly observed. Section 8.4 of Chapter 1, Part IV of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* (1993 version) provides: "The parties in the proceedings shall be given appropriate opportunities to explain and present reasons, especially before a decision unfavorable to the party is made." Since before making Decision No. 1372, which was unfavorable to the retrial applicant Xu Wenqing, there is no evidence that Xu Wenqing was given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons regarding the facts and grounds on which the decision was based, the Patent Reexamination Board violated the procedures stipulated in the *Guidelines for Patent Examination*, which falls under the circumstance of "violation of statutory procedures" as provided in Article 54, Paragraph 2, Subparagraph 3 of the *Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*.

The Patent Reexamination Board and the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, argued that during the invalidation procedure, the retrial applicant Xu Wenqing had already explained and presented reasons regarding the invalidation grounds raised by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, and the outsider, Jinsing Company, that distinguishing features (a) and (b) of claim 1 of the patent in question were not supported by the description and did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law. However, from the facts ascertained, whether in the various statements of opinion Xu Wenqing submitted to the Patent Reexamination Board, including the *Agent's Arguments (Supplement)* submitted on March 10, 1999, or in the "Respondent's Contentions" section summarized in Decision No. 1372, all were directed to the issues raised by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, and the outsider, Jinsing Company, that the "closed-loop circulation system" in distinguishing feature (a) of claim 1 was not closed, and that the various treatment liquids in distinguishing feature (b) were not in a "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow" state. Xu Wenqing was not given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons regarding the invalidation ground on which Decision No. 1372 was based, i.e., "Claim 1 generalizes the method for treating the inner wall of the tube and the method for treating the outer wall of the tube as described in the embodiments of the specification into a treatment method for both the inner and outer walls of the tube."

The Patent Reexamination Board and the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, also argued that during the oral hearing for the patent in question conducted by the Patent Reexamination Board on March 10, 1999, the retrial applicant Xu Wenqing explained and presented reasons regarding the specific invalidation grounds on which Decision No. 1372 was based, and that the above contents were recorded in the agent's arguments submitted by the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, to the Patent Reexamination Board after the oral hearing. However, this argument is not supported by evidence.

The *Gazette of the Patent Office of the People's Republic of China*, No. 10, published by the former Patent Office of China on July 11, 1996, provides: "During the oral hearing, the presiding member of the panel shall designate a panel member to take notes. If necessary, the panel may request the Patent Reexamination Board to assign a clerk to take notes. The person taking notes shall record important hearing matters into the 'Oral Hearing Record.'" "At the conclusion of the oral hearing, the panel shall have the record read by the parties. The parties have the right to request corrections of errors in the record. After the record is verified as correct, it shall be signed by the parties and placed in the case file." Since the Patent Reexamination Board was unable to provide the "Oral Hearing Record" or other similar evidence regarding the disputed facts, the claim that Xu Wenqing had already been given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons is not accepted by this Court.

In the view of the Patent Reexamination Board and the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, as long as the requestor generally raises the invalidation ground that the patent in question does not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, and the Patent Reexamination Board generally informs in the oral hearing notice that the scope of the oral hearing includes the content that the patent in question does not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, this covers all the specific facts, reasons, and evidence that the patent in question does not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law. Even if the parties in the invalidation procedure have not explained or presented reasons regarding these specific facts, reasons, and evidence, particularly the facts, reasons, and evidence on which the invalidation review decision is based, it is considered that the parties in the invalidation procedure have been given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons, and the principle of hearing has been followed. This understanding is incorrect. Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law is only an abstract provision; the non-compliance of a patent right with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law is only a general ground for declaring the patent right invalid, applicable to all patent rights. Specific to a particular case, the facts, reasons, and evidence for non-compliance with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law are specific and targeted. The so-called giving the parties in the administrative procedure an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons means that in the administrative procedure, the parties must be given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons regarding these specific facts, reasons, and evidence. In particular, the facts, reasons, and evidence on which a decision unfavorable to one party is based must be fully heard regarding the party's statements and defenses. Without specific facts, reasons, and evidence, the parties' explanations and presentations of reasons become non-targeted and thus cannot be made. In this case, in Decision No. 1372 declaring the patent in question invalid, the specific facts and reasons on which it was based were that claim 1 of the patent in question generalized the anti-corrosion treatment methods for the inner and outer walls of the tube bundle into one technical solution, whereas according to the description, the anti-corrosion treatment methods for the inner and outer walls of the tube bundle are two different treatment methods; therefore, the claims were not supported by the description. During the invalidation procedure, the Patent Reexamination Board should have given the retrial applicant Xu Wenqing an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons regarding this specific fact and reason before it could be considered to have followed the principle of hearing as provided in the *Guidelines for Patent Examination*. Relying solely on the fact that the requestor generally raised the invalidation ground that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, and that the Patent Reexamination Board informed the parties in the oral hearing notice that the scope of the oral hearing included the content that the patent in question did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, and then claiming that the parties had been given an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons and that the principle of hearing under the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* had been followed, is not convincing.

Therefore, considering all the facts regarding this disputed issue, the retrial applicant Xu Wenqing's ground for retrial that Decision No. 1372 of the Patent Reexamination Board violated the principle of hearing is more sufficient and persuasive than the rebuttal grounds asserted by the Patent Reexamination Board and the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan. This Court accepts it.

2. Regarding the violation of the principle of the parties' request.

The retrial applicant Xu Wenqing also argued that Decision No. 1372 violated the principle of the parties' request as provided in the *Guidelines for Patent Examination*, on the grounds that during the invalidation procedure, the requestors did not raise the invalidation grounds as set forth on page 4, lines 21-26 of Decision No. 1372; those invalidation grounds were raised by the outsider Wang Yueming. However, from the facts ascertained, although the invalidation grounds stated on page 4, lines 21-26 of Decision No. 1372 are similar in content to the invalidation grounds raised by the outsider Wang Yueming, the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, did indeed raise the above invalidation grounds in his post-oral hearing agent's arguments; it is not that no requestor raised this ground. One cannot say that because another person raised such invalidation grounds, Xing Pengwan cannot raise the same invalidation grounds. The issue is that the Patent Reexamination Board did not forward this new invalidation ground raised by Xing Pengwan to Xu Wenqing and did not give Xu Wenqing an appropriate opportunity to explain and present reasons. That the Patent Reexamination Board consolidated and handled this invalidation ground together with the invalidation request filed by Xing Pengwan before the conclusion of the oral hearing does not violate the provisions of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* regarding the principle of the parties' request. Therefore, Xu Wenqing's ground for retrial that Decision No. 1372 violated the principle of the parties' request under the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* is not sustainable.

(II) Regarding the issue of whether the claims are supported by the description.

Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law provides: "The claims shall be based on the description and shall define the scope of patent protection sought." Article 64, Paragraph 2 of the Implementing Rules of the Patent Law further provides that one of the grounds for requesting a declaration of invalidity of a patent right is that the granted invention-creation does not comply with the provisions of Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law. In other words, for a patent, if its claims are not based on the description, any person may request a declaration of invalidity of that patent.

Section 3.2.1 of Chapter 2, Part II of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* (1993 version) provides for what is meant by "the claims shall be based on the description," namely: "The claims shall be based on the description means that the claims shall be supported by the description. That is, the technical solution for which protection is sought in each claim shall be fully disclosed in the description, meaning the scope of the claims shall not exceed the content described in the description."

The current Section 3.2.1 of Chapter 2, Part II of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination* further clarifies the meaning of "the claims shall be based on the description" as: "The claims shall not only be supported by the description in terms of expression form, but shall also be supported in substance. That is, the technical solution for which protection is sought in each claim in the claims shall be a technical solution that a person skilled in the art can directly obtain or generalize from the content disclosed in the description, and the scope of the claims shall not exceed the content described in the description."

With reference to the above provisions of the *Guidelines for Patent Examination*, to determine whether the claims are based on the description, the main consideration is whether the technical solution for which protection is sought in each claim in the claims is a technical solution that a person skilled in the art can directly obtain or generalize from the content disclosed in the description, and whether the scope of the claims exceeds the content described in the description.

With respect to the patent in this case, its claims record a total of four claims, among which the technical solution for which protection is sought in claim 1 is a collection of three technical features, namely: (1) first forming a phosphating layer on the inner and outer wall surfaces of the steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers, followed by paint coating; i.e., the common feature with the prior art; (2) connecting the steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers, pumps, valve groups, and solution tanks via rubber hoses and iron pipes according to the process flow to form a closed-loop circulation system; i.e., feature (a); (3) during the entire process flow, the various treatment liquids (alkali solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) used to treat the inner and outer wall surfaces of the steel tube bundles of coolers and heat exchangers are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state; i.e., feature (b). To determine whether claim 1 is supported by the description, the key is to see whether the above three technical features can be directly obtained or generalized from the content disclosed in the description.

According to the description in the specification, technical feature (1) is directly described in the fourth paragraph of the specification, i.e., "the concept of the present invention is: ... first form a phosphating layer on the inner and outer walls of the steel tube bundle, then ... select ... coating for painting." In this regard, paragraph 2 of Reason 4 of Decision No. 1372 has already confirmed this. Therefore, technical feature (1) can be directly obtained by a person of ordinary skill in the art from the contents disclosed in the specification. Technical features (a) and (b) are not directly described in the specification, but based on the contents disclosed in the specification, a person of ordinary skill in the art can derive them by generalization.

Specifically, technical feature (a) can be derived by generalization from paragraphs 4, 6, and 7 of the specification and the drawings. Paragraph 4 of the specification records: "operated by connecting pumps, valves, pipelines, and solution tanks according to the process flow"; paragraph 6 records the description of the drawings; paragraph 7 respectively records the embodiments of the anti-corrosion treatment methods for the inner and outer walls of the tubes; the accompanying drawing of the specification illustrates the connection of steel tube bundles, pumps, valve groups, and solution tanks via rubber hoses and iron pipes according to the process flow. Through the above contents disclosed in the specification, a person of ordinary skill in the art can completely generalize that: acid solution tank A, valve 2, valve 1, rubber hose JG, pump, G1, cooler, G2, JG, hydrochloric acid tank inlet a, and acid solution tank A constitute a closed-loop circulation system for the pickling step; close valve 5, open valves 6 and 7, ... move the rubber hose to connect to the outlet pipe e of tank E, and phosphating solution tank E, valve 7, valve 6, valve 1, JG, pump, G1, cooler, G2, JG, phosphating solution tank inlet e, and phosphating solution tank E constitute a closed-loop circulation system for the phosphating step; alkali solution tank B, valve 3, valve 1, JG, alkali solution tank inlet, and alkali solution tank B constitute a closed-loop circulation system for the alkali cleaning step. By generalizing the above three closed-loop circulation systems of alkali cleaning, pickling, and phosphating, the technical feature described in distinguishing feature (a) can be derived: "connecting the cooler, heat exchanger metal steel tube bundle, pump, valve group, and solution tanks via rubber hoses and iron pipes according to the process flow to form a closed-loop circulation system."

Technical feature (b) can be derived by generalization from the inner and outer wall treatment processes described in paragraph 7 of the specification. For example, from the pickling closed-loop circulation system, it can be known that the acid solution is in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state according to the closed-loop circulation system of the pickling step; from the phosphating closed-loop circulation system, it can be known that the phosphating solution is in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state according to the closed-loop circulation system of the phosphating step; from the alkali cleaning closed-loop circulation system, it can be known that the alkali solution is in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state according to the closed-loop circulation system of the alkali cleaning step.

Thus, it can be seen that technical feature (1) of claim 1 of the invention patent in this case is directly described in the specification, and technical features (a) and (b) can be derived by a person of ordinary skill in the art from the contents disclosed in the specification through generalization. When these three technical features are combined, they exactly disclose the technical solution sought to be protected by claim 1 and do not exceed the contents recorded in the specification. Therefore, claim 1 is supported by the specification.

Not only is claim 1 supported by the specification, but the technical solutions recorded in claims 2, 3, and 4 can also be derived from the specification by generalization. Therefore, claims 2, 3, and 4 are also supported by the specification.

The main reason why Decision No. 1372 considered that the patent claims in this case were not based on the specification was that the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the embodiments of the specification were not the same technical solution, and it was inappropriate for claim 1 to generalize them into one technical solution, thus failing to obtain support from the specification. However, this reason is difficult to sustain.

The Examination Guidelines (1993 version), Part 2, Chapter 2, Section 225 stipulates that a claim records a collection of technical solutions whose technical features are common characteristics. As long as the technical solutions share all the common features in the claim, they can be generalized together to form one claim and be regarded as one technical solution. As stated above, the common features of the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the embodiments of the specification in this case are: (1) using the same process step of "first forming a phosphating layer, then applying paint coating"; (2) using the same equipment conditions, i.e., the "closed-loop circulation system" described in feature (a) of claim 1; (3) using the same process conditions, i.e., all treatment liquids described in feature (b) of claim 1 are in a "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state." Therefore, from the perspective of patent law, the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments belong to the same technical solution, not two different technical solutions. It is not improper for claim 1 to generalize the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method described in the specification embodiments into a method for treating inner and outer walls, and such generalization complies with the relevant provisions of the Examination Guidelines.

The Examination Guidelines (1993 version), Part 2, Chapter 2, Section 3.3, paragraph 8 stipulates: "If supported by the specification, a claim is allowed to define an invention or utility model by way of generalization." It also specifies two methods of generalization: generic concept generalization and parallel selection generalization. As far as the patent in this case is concerned, the feature in the preamble of claim 1, "first forming a phosphating layer, then applying paint coating," is a generalization of the specific process steps used in the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments. For example, the specific process steps used in the pre-paint surface treatment of the inner wall, such as sandblasting, pickling, water washing, neutralization, phosphating, water washing, drying, etc., and the specific process steps used in the pre-paint surface treatment of the outer wall, such as alkali cleaning, water washing, pickling, water washing, neutralization, phosphating, water washing, drying, etc., are all generalized by the generic concept "first forming a phosphating layer"; feature (a) of claim 1, "connecting the cooler, heat exchanger metal steel tube bundle, pump, valve group, and solution tanks via rubber hoses and iron pipes according to the process flow to form a closed-loop circulation system," is a generalization of the "closed-loop circulation system" formed by the specific equipment connection methods used in the pickling and phosphating steps in the inner wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments and the "closed-loop circulation system" formed by the specific equipment connection methods used in the alkali cleaning, pickling, and phosphating steps in the outer wall treatment method; feature (b), "the various treatment liquids (alkali solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) used for treating the inner and outer wall surfaces of the cooler and heat exchanger metal steel tube bundles in the entire process flow are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state," is a generalization of the condition that the acid solution and phosphating solution used in the inner wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments are "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state" and the condition that the alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution used in the outer wall treatment method are "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state." By using the above three generic concepts, i.e., the common features of the inner and outer wall treatment methods, to generalize the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method described in the specification embodiments into an inner and outer wall treatment method, this not only meets the requirement of conciseness for claims but also does not exceed the contents recorded in the specification.

The differences in the specific process steps of pre-paint surface treatment between the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments, such as the inner wall using sandblasting and the outer wall using alkali cleaning, and the resulting differences in related process steps, i.e., the differences described in paragraph 1 of Reason 4 of Decision No. 1372, are only specific to that embodiment and cannot be taken to mean that the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method are two different technical solutions that cannot be generalized in one claim. Under the premise that the technical subject and the features in the preamble are the same, as long as the equipment used in the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method both have the common feature of being connected to form a "closed-loop circulation system" and the treatment liquids used both have the common feature of being "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state," they should be considered the same technical solution within the meaning of patent law and can be generalized in one claim.

The reason why Decision No. 1372 considered that the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments were two different technical solutions and that it was inappropriate for claim 1 to generalize them into an inner and outer wall treatment method was mainly due to an erroneous determination of the technical contribution of the patent in this case and an erroneous interpretation of feature (b) of claim 1.

First, Decision No. 1372 considered that "compared with the prior art, the technical contribution of the patent in this case lies in the process steps rather than the process conditions," and this lacks sufficient evidence.

From the facts ascertained by this court, the process steps for forming a phosphating layer, i.e., pre-paint surface treatment, such as sandblasting, pickling, water washing, neutralization, phosphating, water washing, drying, painting, or alkali cleaning, water washing, pickling, water washing, neutralization, phosphating, water washing, drying, painting, etc., as well as the selection between sandblasting and alkali cleaning based on different treatment objects, are all prior art. Moreover, these have been written by the petitioner for retrial, Xu Wenqing, into the preamble of claim 1.

The third party in the original trial, Xing Pengwan, also argued in the invalidation proceeding that the pre-paint surface treatment of metals was "common knowledge in coating technology." Although Xing Pengwan further argued during the trial of this court that the process steps for forming a phosphating layer disclosed in the relevant publications were only specific individual steps, which could be arbitrarily combined and were not a complete set of process steps, and thus could not prove that the process steps for forming a phosphating layer were prior art, this defense cannot stand. Although the process steps for forming a phosphating layer disclosed in the above publications are not completely consistent with the process steps for forming a phosphating layer disclosed in the embodiments of the specification of the patent in this case—for example, the inner wall uses sandblasting and the outer wall uses alkali cleaning—selecting different treatment methods for different contaminants is exactly the technical content disclosed in the above publications, and a person of ordinary skill in the art would be able to conceive of this based on the teachings of the prior art.

Therefore, the contribution of the invention patent in this case to the prior art is not the specific process steps for forming a phosphating layer; its true technical contribution lies in proposing a dynamic treatment method for "forming a phosphating layer," namely features (a) and (b) of claim 1. The technical feature recorded in feature (a)—connecting the cooler, heat exchanger metal steel tube bundle, pump, valve group, and solution tanks via rubber hoses and iron pipes according to the process flow to form a closed-loop circulation system—is the equipment condition required to achieve "forming a phosphating layer"; the technical feature recorded in feature (b)—the various treatment liquids for treating the inner and outer walls of the cooler and heat exchanger steel tube bundles, i.e., the alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution in parentheses, are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state—is the condition under which a phosphating layer is formed through the continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow of various treatment liquids, i.e., the process condition. According to the process flow of forming a phosphating layer, through the equipment condition of feature (a) and the process condition of feature (b), the inner and outer walls of the steel tube bundle form a phosphating layer during dynamic treatment, i.e., a dynamic treatment method. Through this dynamic treatment method, positive effects such as high temperature resistance, extended equipment service life, short anti-corrosion treatment period, and low cost can be achieved, overcoming shortcomings in the prior art such as poor adhesion between the coating and the metal steel substrate and long anti-corrosion treatment periods.

It is precisely because Decision No. 1372 erroneously determined the contribution of the invention patent in this case to the prior art as being the process steps, rather than the equipment condition of feature (a) and the process condition of feature (b) of claim 1, that it directly led to the following conclusions in that decision: (1) The differences in the specific process steps of pre-paint surface treatment between the inner wall and the outer wall described in the specification embodiments are two different technical solutions that cannot be generalized in one claim; (2) The use of alkali treatment liquid when treating the inner wall, the non-use of alkali treatment liquid when treating the outer wall, and the omission of the hot water washing step after alkali cleaning for the outer wall have effects that are "difficult to predetermine and evaluate," and the use of alkali for neutralization is a generalization of "various alkalis"; (3) Claim 1 does not include the specific process steps "sandblasting, neutralization, and drying" for the inner wall treatment and "the temperature and time of the alkali treatment liquid, hot water washing, and drying steps" for the outer wall treatment as recorded in the specification embodiments, making it "an incomplete and inappropriately generalized technical solution."

However, if the technical contribution of the patent in this case is correctly identified as the equipment condition of feature (a) and the process condition of feature (b) of claim 1, it is not difficult to find that:

(1) The technical solutions for treating the inner and outer walls are generalized by higher-level concepts, such as the common process step "first forming a phosphating layer, then applying paint coating," the common equipment condition of a "closed-loop circulation system," and the common process condition that "various treatment liquids (alkali solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state," and thus constitute the same technical solution. The differences in specific process steps between the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method recorded in the specification embodiments are merely differences between specific embodiments under the technical solution generalized by claim 1 and have no substantial impact on determining whether the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method are the same technical solution.

(2) Based on the teachings of the prior art on pre-paint surface treatment, such as the selective use of alkali cleaning and sandblasting depending on the treatment object, and the hot and cold water washing steps after alkali cleaning, a person of ordinary skill in the art would be fully capable of predetermining and evaluating the effects of using alkali treatment liquid for the inner wall, not using alkali treatment liquid for the outer wall, and omitting the hot water washing step after alkali cleaning for the outer wall.

Neutralization refers to adding alkali to an acidic solution or adding acid to an alkaline solution to make the solution neutral, i.e., pH 7. This is common knowledge in the art. The alkali used for neutralization is not the same concept as the alkali treatment liquid used in the alkali cleaning step. A person of ordinary skill in the art, based on common general knowledge in the art, would be able to distinguish the alkali used for neutralization from the alkali treatment liquid and would not understand it as a generalization covering various alkalis including the alkali treatment liquid.

(3) The pre-paint surface treatment process steps for the inner and outer walls, including the temperature and time of the alkali solution and the selective use of sandblasting and alkali cleaning depending on the treatment object, which are all prior art, have been generalized by the phrase "first forming a phosphating layer" recorded in the preamble of claim 1. According to the provisions of the Examination Guidelines, these prior art features need not and should not be written into the characterizing portion of claim 1. The Examination Guidelines (1993 version), Part 2, Chapter 2, Section 3.3.1, paragraph 6 stipulates: "In the preamble of an independent claim, only those known technical features closely related to the subject matter of the invention or utility model need to be stated." Paragraph 7 stipulates: "In the characterizing portion of an independent claim, the distinguishing technical features different from the known technical features among the essential technical features of the invention or utility model shall be recorded." Therefore, claim 1, which "omits the process steps of sandblasting, neutralization, and drying" and "for the outer wall, omits the temperature and time of the alkali treatment liquid, hot water washing, and drying steps," is still a complete and appropriately generalized technical solution.

Second, the interpretation by Decision No. 1372 of distinguishing feature (b) of claim 1 does not conform to its true content and violates the principles of claim interpretation stipulated in the Patent Law.

That decision considered that, compared with the specification embodiments, the technical solution recorded in claim 1 "does not use alkali treatment liquid when treating the inner wall surface," "also omits the process steps of sandblasting, neutralization, and drying," and "for the outer wall, omits the temperature and time of the alkali treatment liquid, hot water washing, and drying steps, making it also an incomplete and inappropriately generalized technical solution for the outer wall." This essentially interprets feature (b) of claim 1 as process steps, with the written order of the alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution in parentheses representing the process sequence of alkali cleaning-pickling-phosphating, and both the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method must adopt the same process steps and use the same treatment liquids, i.e., alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution.

The Patent Reexamination Board and the third party in the original trial, Xing Pengwan, expressed this even more clearly in their relevant submissions. For example, the Patent Reexamination Board stated in its second-instance submissions: "The order of process steps generalized in claim 1 (alkali cleaning, pickling, phosphating) is inconsistent with the pickling and phosphating disclosed in the specification. Therefore, the generalization of the order of process steps in claim 1 is unreasonable and not supported by the specification." The third party, Xing Pengwan, also stated in his submissions to this court that regarding the alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution in distinguishing technical feature (b) of claim 1, "a person of ordinary skill in the art would naturally understand ... alkali cleaning first, then pickling, and finally phosphating."

Since Decision No. 1372 interpreted the "various treatment liquids," i.e., alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution, in feature (b) of claim 1 as the process sequence of alkali cleaning-pickling-phosphating, requiring both the inner wall and the outer wall to adopt the same process steps and use the same treatment liquids, then it would naturally be considered inappropriate for feature (b) to generalize the inner wall treatment method (which does not use alkali liquid) and the outer wall treatment method (which uses alkali liquid), along with the resulting differences in corresponding process steps, into an inner and outer wall treatment method.

However, the above interpretation by Decision No. 1372 does not conform to the true content of distinguishing feature (b) of claim 1. Such a practice of interpreting the claims separate from the specification contravenes the principles of claim interpretation stipulated in the Patent Law.

Article 56, Paragraph 1 of the Patent Law stipulates: "The extent of protection of the invention or utility model patent shall be determined by the terms of the claims. The description and the drawings may be used to interpret the claims." Therefore, claims should be interpreted in conjunction with the description and the drawings. From the literal meaning of the patent claims in this case, distinguishing feature (b) of claim 1 does not directly state that the written order of the three treatment liquids is the process order, nor that the inner and outer walls of the steel tube bundle must both simultaneously adopt the same process steps and use the same treatment liquids. It merely indicates that the three treatment liquids, i.e., alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution, are in a "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state." From the specification embodiments, the inner wall uses pickling and phosphating, i.e., uses acid solution and phosphating solution; the outer wall uses alkali cleaning, pickling, and phosphating, i.e., uses alkali solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution. Clearly, the specification also does not describe that the written order of the three treatment liquids is the process order, nor that the inner wall and the outer wall must both simultaneously adopt the same process steps and use the same treatment liquids.

Therefore, based on the literal meaning of distinguishing feature (b) of Claim 1 and in conjunction with the content described in the specification, the correct interpretation of distinguishing feature (b) of Claim 1 should be: There are three types of treatment liquids for the inner and outer walls of the processing tube, namely alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution. These three treatment liquids must be in a "continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state." As long as they are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state, regardless of whether the inner wall and outer wall of the tube simultaneously use the three treatment liquids, it falls within the scope covered by distinguishing feature (b). This being the case, since the embodiments of the specification have already indicated that whether it is the acid solution and phosphating solution used for the inner wall of the tube, or the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution used for the outer wall of the tube, their common feature is being in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state, then the generalization of feature (b) of Claim 1 is certainly supported by the specification.

The Patent Reexamination Board and the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, repeatedly argued that the technical contribution of the patent in question lies in the process steps; that the method for treating the inner wall of the tube and the method for treating the outer wall of the tube described in the embodiments of the specification are different technical solutions; that the textual order of "alkaline solution, acid solution, phosphating solution" within the parentheses of feature (b) of Claim 1 should be interpreted as a process sequence, and the inner and outer walls of the steel tube bundle must adopt the same process steps and use the same treatment liquids; and that Claim 1 inappropriately generalizes the inner wall treatment method and the outer wall treatment method into one technical solution, which is not supported by the specification, among other reasons. However, as discussed above, these reasons all lack factual and legal basis and are difficult to sustain.

The third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, further argued that the various treatment liquids (alkaline solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) for treating the inner and outer walls of the tube are not in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state, because during the process, when liquids are changed, the later liquid must "push out" the earlier liquid from the equipment being treated; that the "water rinsing" step, as a necessary technical feature for achieving the purpose of the invention, was not written into the claims, and "water" itself is not a liquid in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state. During the court hearing, it was also argued that when performing the coating application step in the specification embodiments, the cooler is not connected to any other components, which is inconsistent with feature (a) of Claim 1.

In fact, regarding "the various treatment liquids (alkaline solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state" stated in feature (b) of Claim 1, for a person skilled in the art, after carefully reading the specification, it is easy to understand that this refers to the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution themselves being "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state," rather than referring to the state between the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution as being "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state." In the transition process between the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution, there will naturally be certain temporal and spatial gaps. The specification embodiments have already described this in detail. Even if feature (b) of Claim 1 does not explicitly state that "the various treatment liquids (alkaline solution, acid solution, phosphating solution) are in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state" means that the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution themselves are "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state," a person skilled in the art would not misunderstand this.

Although Claim 1 does not directly include the "water rinsing" step between the alkaline washing, acid washing, and phosphating steps, since the "water rinsing" step is prior art and is already summarized by the feature "forming a phosphating layer" in the preamble of Claim 1, a person skilled in the art, based on the teachings of the prior art, is fully capable of understanding this. As held in Decision No. 1372, a complete chemical cleaning process should include three main stages: alkaline washing, acid washing, and passivation, and each stage requires water rinsing as a transition. "A person of ordinary skill in the art who masters the prior art and common knowledge can understand and identify the water rinsing steps between the acid washing, alkaline washing, and phosphating steps." As for the water used in the water rinsing step, it is not a treatment liquid as referred to in feature (b) of Claim 1. The treatment liquids referred to in feature (b) of Claim 1 are specifically the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution. Whether the water used in the water rinsing step is "in a continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state" is irrelevant to this case.

By the same reasoning, since feature (a) of Claim 1 is intended to provide the equipment conditions necessary for achieving the continuous and uninterrupted circulating flow state of the various treatment liquids, i.e., the alkaline solution, acid solution, and phosphating solution, and is not directed to the coating application, whether the cooler is connected to other components to form a closed-loop circulation system during coating application has no bearing on determining whether the claims of the patent in question are supported by the specification.

Xing Pengwan also argued that the *Examination Guidelines* (1993 text) did not stipulate that whether a "person skilled in the art" can identify the technical solution recorded in the claims from the specification should be used as the basis for determining whether the claims are supported by the specification. Therefore, the applicant for retrial's argument that the technical solution for which protection is sought by the claims of the patent in question can be summarized or identified by a person skilled in the art from the content disclosed in the specification lacks legal basis. It should be noted that the first paragraph of Section 3.2.1 of Part Two, Chapter 2 of the *Examination Guidelines* (1993 text), concerning the meaning of "based on the specification," indeed does not literally contain the phrase that whether a "person skilled in the art" can identify the technical solution recorded in the claims from the specification is used as the basis for determining whether the claims are supported by the specification. However, that paragraph stipulates that "if the technical solution for which protection is sought by each claim is fully disclosed in the specification, i.e., the scope of the claim does not exceed the content described in the specification," then the claim can be considered supported by the specification. The so-called "fully disclosed" naturally includes two situations: where the technical solution for which protection is sought by the claims is directly described in the specification, and where a person skilled in the art can summarize or identify it from the content disclosed in the specification. In fact, the Patent Reexamination Board has consistently applied this in its examination practice. For example, the second paragraph of the Reasoning section of Decision No. 189 on the Request for Declaration of Invalidity made by the Patent Reexamination Board on November 23, 1991, states: "The provision of Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law that 'the claims shall be based on the specification' means that the claims must be supported by the specification, i.e., the subject matter for which protection is sought by each claim must be explained in the specification or can be summarized by a person of ordinary skill in the art... from the content described in the specification, or can be understood." The current *Examination Guidelines*, in the first paragraph of Section 321 of Part Two, Chapter 2, further clearly defines the meaning of the provision of Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law that "the claims shall be based on the specification" based on summarizing the experience of patent examination practice. Therefore, the applicant for retrial's argument that the technical solution for which protection is sought by the claims of the patent in question can be summarized by a person skilled in the art from the content disclosed in the specification and is supported by the specification is well-founded. The rebuttal argument of the third party at first instance, Xing Pengwan, on this point is also difficult to sustain.

It should be pointed out that the drafting of the claims and the specification of the patent in question indeed has certain defects.
